“You don’t need carbon fiber, custom cycling apparel, or a support crew to conquer massive distances. You just need a solid bike, a plan, and the mental grit to push through.”
On November 29, 2025, I set out on a mission to test the absolute limits of raw human willpower. The objective? Complete an unsupported 300-kilometer ultra-endurance loop across Malaysia in under 24 hours.
The twist? No $10,000 carbon fiber road bike, no aerodynamic Lycra bibs, no clipless pedals, and strictly zero support crew following in a van with spare wheels and ice packs. Just me, a lower mid-range DIY gravel bike, regular casual sportswear, hiking shoes, and a 4 kg backpack weighing down on my shoulders for nearly a full day.
1. The Failure That Fueled the Ride Every major physical achievement is built on the ashes of a previous failure.
Six weeks prior, on October 12, 2025, I made my first attempt at this 300 km goal. I was in the rhythm, clocking an average speed I was proud of, until Kilometer 120.1. Without warning, my gear shifter snapped with a harsh metallic click. Stranded with an unshiftable drivetrain after 5 hours and 5 minutes of solid riding, I was forced to retire early. Leaving that route unfinished burned in my mind every single day. I brought the bike home, rebuilt the broken components piece by piece, and waited for my shot at redemption.
Mental grit was tested again just seven days before this second attempt. During a 100 km night training session, I rode straight into the fresh scene of a fatal road accident. A victim was lying motionless on the asphalt surrounded by shattered glass and pooling blood. Passing within inches of that raw tragedy anchored a cold reality into my mind: Malaysian roads at night do not forgive mistakes.
2. Rules of the Challenge: Self-Imposed Hard Mode To truly isolate mental resilience from equipment advantage, I bound myself to a strict set of self-imposed rules:
The Bike: DIY Lower Mid-Range Gravel Bike—heavy, mechanical, and far from aerodynamic. The Attire: 100% Casual Gear. A basic dri-fit shirt, regular athletic shorts (zero padded chamois), sturdy hiking shoes on flat pedals, and no technical cycling gear. The Setup (100% Solo & Unsupported): A 3.1 kg to 4.5 kg weighted backpack strapped to my back the entire distance (no panniers or full frame bag system to lighten the load on my spine). A small Bluetooth speaker mounted to the handlebar stem for ambient audio. Strictly no escort vehicles, no pacing partners, and no planned roadside pit crews. 3. Route & Key Performance Stats Date & Start Time: 03:45 AM, Saturday, 29 November 2025 Start Location: Klang Municipal Council (MPK), Selangor, Malaysia Total Distance: 298.09 km Moving Time: 12h 53m 32s Elapsed Time: 23h 17m 26s (Sub-24 Hours Achieved!) Elevation Gain: 1,736 m Average Speed: 23.1 km/h (Max Speed: 53.6 km/h) Energy Output: 6,630 kJ / 143 W Avg Power (7,392 Calories burned) [Klang Start] ➔ [Banting] ➔ [Nilai] ➔ [Seremban] ➔ [Alor Gajah] ➔ [Malacca] ➔ [Coastal Route / Lukut] ➔ [Port Dickson] ➔ [Sepang / KLIA Wasteland] ➔ [Finish] 4. Why Reject Lycra, Carbon, and Support Crews? Modern cycling culture dictates that to ride 300 km, you must spend thousands on ultralight carbon frames, skin-tight aero jerseys, super-stiff carbon-soled shoes, and thick bib pads to prevent saddle sores. Ultra-distance riders usually rely on support cars following behind with cold water, fresh meals, and spare tubes.
Beyond proving that endurance is driven by heart rather than top-tier equipment, this challenge was deeply personal: it was about conquering a defining dream of my 20s.
Your twenties are a unique chapter in life—a window of time where your time, energy, and freedom belong entirely to you. Once you transition into your thirties, life naturally shifts, and family becomes the primary focus and top priority. Before taking on those future responsibilities, I wanted to take full ownership of my youth, push my absolute limits, and achieve something unforgettable. I wanted to build a story worth telling—so that decades from now, I can look my future children in the eyes and tell them what was possible when their parent refused to back down.
Choosing to carry a heavy 4 kg backpack meant my shoulders, lower back, and sit bones bore relentless downward force for 23 straight hours. Every watt saved by aerodynamic gear was a watt I had to produce manually through pure grit.
5. The Journey: Darkness, Floods, Crashes, and Wastelands 03:45 AM — Rolling into the Unknown Leaving Klang Municipal Council under the dim glow of orange streetlights, the night air was heavy with humidity. The route cut south toward the quiet, wide avenues of Putrajaya before weaving toward Seremban and the historic coastal approaches of Malacca.
Battling Active Flood Zones in Malacca What the weather app didn’t capture was that parts of Malacca were actively submerged under severe flash floods. Emergency relief centers (PPS) were opening up across multiple districts.
As I pushed into low-lying rural stretches, heavy rain clouds hung low, turning the air ice-cold. Spray from passing lorries cut visibility, and murky floodwaters encroached onto the asphalt. Navigating submerged edges where potholes were completely hidden required hyper-vigilance—one wrong line meant a ruined rim or a plunge into a roadside ditch. Knowing a single heavy downpour could trap me in a flooded dead-end added intense mental friction to every pedal stroke.
Crossing the 200 km Milestone & Resting at Port Dickson By the time I hit the 200 km mark, exhaustion was taking its toll, but the route was leading back along the coastal stretch towards Port Dickson. Taking a brief breather on the beach gave me a moment to recalibrate before facing the darkest night section ahead.
Blinding High Beams, a Sudden Crash, and Pitch Darkness Midway through the ride, while navigating a pitch-black rural road with zero street lamps, disaster struck.
A vehicle approached from behind at high speed, blasting blinding high beams straight into my mirrors and eye line. Completely blinded by the glare, I swerved slightly toward the shoulder to yield. In an instant, my front tire dropped into a massive, jagged pothole.
The handlebars twisted violently out of my grip. I went flying over the bars, slamming hard onto the pavement.
The car didn’t stop—its taillights vanished into the distance, leaving me lying alone in dead silence on an unlit road. Dazed and bleeding from minor abrasions, I checked the bike under the faint glow of my headlamp. The front wheel had taken a direct impact and was jammed sideways against the fork frame; the mechanical shifting was severely misaligned.
Standing alone in total dark, heart pounding with adrenaline, I wrestled the front wheel back into place, re-trued it as best as I could with manual leverage, adjusted the brake calipers, and clipped back in. Quitting wasn’t on the itinerary.
The 40 km Wasteland: Lukut to Sepang (12:00 AM – 3:00 AM) The darkest mental zone occurred between midnight and 3:00 AM along the 40-kilometer stretch connecting Lukut to Sepang and KLIA.
Over 95% of this corridor had no operational streetlights. Dense, overgrown oil palm trees and jungle canopy absorbed what little moonlight existed. Petrol stations were locked up tight, offering no lights or water refills.
To keep mind-numbing fatigue from taking over, I cranked the volume on my mounted Bluetooth speaker, letting music punch through the heavy silence. The road felt like an apocalyptic wasteland: across the entire 300 km journey, I counted between 30 to 50 dead animal carcasses strewn across the road—stray dogs, cats, massive monitor lizards, and at one point, three full-sized cows lying dead on a single stretch of shoulder.
6. The Ultimate Crucible: Hidden Agony & Mental Strain If anyone were to ask me what the single hardest part of those 23 hours was, the answer wouldn’t be physical exhaustion—it was the extreme physical torment combined with a state of hyper-vigilant mental strain.
Forgoing professional cycling bibs proved to be the most brutal sacrifice of the entire challenge. Without a padded chamois to cushion the impact, hundreds of thousands of pedal strokes and relentless friction reduced the skin on my inner thighs to raw, inflamed agony. By the second half of the ride, every single revolution felt like a dull blade sawing through open flesh. That deep, bone-chilling pain forced me to stop every few minutes, leaning over my handlebars by the roadside to let the searing burn fade just enough before gritting my teeth and mounting the saddle once more.
Yet, even more punishing than the physical torture was the suffocating mental exhaustion.
Along dozens of kilometers of unlit roads, the pitch-black night swallowed the highway whole. I had to stretch my focus to its absolute limit, unable to relax my eyes for even a fraction of a second. At any moment, a deep, bone-breaking pothole could appear out of nowhere, stray dogs or wildlife could dart across the lane, or a massive animal carcass might lie sprawled across the asphalt. In the cold and dark, I wasn’t just fighting fatigue—I was playing a high-stakes game against potential disaster. Maintaining that level of intense concentration under constant high pressure drained my mental bandwidth far faster than muscle fatigue ever could.
7. The Chaotic Aftermath & Logistical Survival Crossing the 298 km mark at 23 hours and 17 minutes, I officially completed the challenge within the 24-hour limit. I was exhausted, filthy, and covered in road grime—yet surging on post-ride adrenaline. Instead of slumping onto the curb, I decided to celebrate with a bizarre change of pace: pushing my dusty bike straight into KLIA2 to shop around and grab food among stunned airport travelers.
The final logistical stretch proved to be its own mini-adventure:
The Check-In Fiasco: Battered by friction skin irritation and desperate for a shower, I booked a hotel room online, assuming “same-day check-in” meant immediate access. Arriving at the desk, I was met with a strict 2:00 PM check-in policy at a fully booked hotel. Eventually, I found a room at Hotel Night Queen, collapsing for a brief 1.5-hour power nap between 2:50 PM and 4:30 PM. Bike Security Paranoia: Having no heavy lock, I had to lock the gravel bike through its frame and wheels outside open public spots—staring out the window every few minutes to ensure it wasn’t being loaded into a van. The Train Breakdown Commute: Planning to catch a direct KTM train home to Klang, I was hit with major service disruptions. I had to detour to Kajang, manually haul my heavy bike up staircases, and board the MRT line toward KL Sentral before finally reaching home. 8. Final Reflection & Declaration: Where Is the Limit? Bouncing back from a snapped shifter on my first attempt, surviving a high-speed night crash, navigating active flood zones, and pushing through 300 km of pitch-black roads proved what I set out to test:
You don’t need elite gear to achieve extraordinary endurance milestones.
When you strip away the carbon frames, the custom apparel, and the safety net of a support crew, all that remains is your relationship with pain and your willingness to keep turning the pedals.
If you were to strip away all these negative variables—if I didn’t have to haul a 4 kg weighted backpack on my spine; if I didn’t have to worry about running out of food and water; if I didn’t have to ride in constant fear of hidden road hazards in the dark and floodwaters; and if you handed me a top-tier carbon road bike, a dedicated support vehicle trailing behind, and seamless roadside logistics—
I am absolute in my conviction that I could have pushed straight through to 500 kilometers that very same day.
This grueling 300 km journey proved what mattered most: it is never the limit of physical endurance that holds us back, but the constraints of our environment. As long as the fire inside refuses to burn out, these legs will keep carrying me further.
summary:
“You don’t need carbon fiber, custom cycling apparel, or a support crew to conquer massive distances. You just need a solid bike, a plan, and the mental grit to push through.”

content:
When you roll out of your driveway at 2:00 AM carrying a heavy backpack on a solo gravel bike, you know you aren’t just going for a casual weekend ride. You’re signing up for an endurance test. What started as a goal to conquer Fraser’s Hill turned into a 20-hour marathon filled with pitch-black detours, surprise wildlife encounters, mechanical setbacks, and moments of unexpected camaraderie.
Here is the story of how 200 kilometers and pure grit pushed me to my absolute limits.
Key Stats & Details Route: Klang Bukit Tinggi → Fraser’s Hill → Batang Kali (Train) → Klang (Train) → Klang Bukit Tinggi Total Elapsed Time: 20 hours, 23 minutes Moving Time: 9 hours, 2 minutes Total Distance: ~200 km (191.74 km recorded + 8 km extra) Elevation Gain: 2,208 m Setup: DIY Gravel Bike + 4.2 kg–6 kg Backpack 1. Into the Pitch Black: 4:00 AM Detours & Stealth Cows Fueled only by a single McDonald’s chicken wrap in Klang, I pushed into the night. Just two hours into the ride, around 4:00 AM, my navigation led me into a dense, heavily wooded area.
For 45 long, heart-pounding minutes, I was navigating a pitch-black forest alone. Every rustle in the trees sounded amplified. Just as I managed to fight my way back toward the road, the darkness threw another wild surprise at me: two pitch-black cows materialized out of nowhere, standing inches from my handlebars. They were so close I could have reached out and touched them before my brain even registered they were there.
2. Running on Fumes: Flat Tires & Latching onto Pros No epic ride comes without mechanical drama—a flat tire forced an unexpected pit stop, putting a dent in my momentum. Worse yet, I missed my last chance to grab a proper meal before starting the heavy climbing toward Fraser’s Hill.
Remarkably, I covered the first 110 km on an almost completely empty stomach, running solely on that initial chicken wrap and a tiny 50-gram bag of nuts.
At kilometer 110, exhausted and running on pure fumes, a professional cycling team flew past me. Instead of dropping back, I dug deep into my reserves, latched onto their wheel train, and held their brisk training pace for an exhilarating 15 to 17 minutes. It was the ultimate mental reset right when I needed it most.
3. Conquering Fraser’s Hill & Finding Community Reaching the summit at Fraser’s Hill felt like a monumental triumph. At the top, the solo journey briefly turned social. I randomly met four fellow cyclists, and together we shared a well-deserved meal, rested our legs, and took in the sights before starting the journey back down.
4. The 30 km Vehicle Draft & The Final Stretch The downhill stretch brought its own thrill. Heading down toward Batang Kali, I managed to position myself behind a vehicle moving at a steady pace, drafting behind it for a thrilling 25 to 30 km descent.
By this point, however, the heavy backpack had taken a massive toll on my shoulders and back, forcing me to pull over periodically just to stretch out the muscle fatigue. After coasting down to Batang Kali, I caught the train back to Klang, before pedaling the final stretch back home to Bukit Tinggi, rolling in at 10:30 PM.
Final Thoughts Looking back at the GPS map, the numbers tell one story: 2,208 meters of climbing and over 9 hours in the saddle. But the real memory is in the moments between the numbers—the quiet anxiety of a dark forest, the thrill of holding a pro pace on empty tanks, and the sheer relief of making it back in one piece.
It was grueling, unpredictable, and unforgettable. Exactly what gravel riding is all about.

If I had to choose the most brutally difficult course in my entire self-learning journey, it would undoubtedly be the Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree (SDCND).
Born in 1996 with only a Diploma in Business Studies, I had zero Computer Science (CS) background. I had never taken university-level advanced math or higher physics. Yet, I not only conquered this Autonomous Driving program—a course that leaves many CS master’s students struggling—but also became one of its top early graduates globally.
Here is the story of my “unconventional” path, how winning #1 in MIT’s DeepTraffic competition funded my tuition, and why the Udacity SDCND was the hardest—and coolest—course I’ve ever taken.
1. A Business Student’s Unconventional Start in Code My passion for programming wasn’t sparked in a university lecture hall.
During my years studying Business, I realized I was far more fascinated by code and technology than business theory. Lacking formal resources, I turned entirely to self-directed learning:
Scrappy Foundations: I learned computer basics on Alison and picked up coding syntax on SoloLearn and W3Schools. Curious about what “real CS majors” learned, I reached out to my high school classmates in university, asking for their course syllabi and lecture slides. I’m still deeply grateful for how generously they shared them with me. Learning by Doing: After building a foundation in web development, I started using WordPress to build websites for relatives and friends. Word spread, and I eventually took on freelance gigs creating official websites for local small businesses and manufacturing companies. Right before graduating, I researched industry trends and studied the journeys of legendary builders. I noticed a recurring, powerful realization: the best software engineers and technical innovators are ultimately self-taught.
I was deeply inspired by iconic founders and developers who reshaped the industry without traditional Computer Science paths or by venturing far beyond standard curricula:
Evan You (Creator of Vue.js) & John Resig (Creator of jQuery) — both coming from non-traditional CS backgrounds (Art & Art History / Computer Science with a strong self-taught open-source ethos) to craft frameworks that revolutionized modern web development globally. Drew Houston & Arash Ferdowsi (Co-founders of Dropbox) — who turned raw self-directed problem-solving and persistent iteration into seamless cloud infrastructure used by millions. Chris Wanstrath (Co-founder of GitHub) — an English major dropout who taught himself to code and built the world’s largest platform for software collaboration. Jan Koum (Co-founder of WhatsApp) — who self-studied computer networking from purchased manuals and rebuilt messaging infrastructure for the entire globe. Palmer Luckey (Founder of Oculus VR) — a self-taught hardware tinkerer who built early VR prototypes in his garage, reigniting the modern virtual reality revolution. Mike Krieger (Co-founder of Instagram) — who bridged Symbolic Systems and self-taught software engineering to build scalable systems for billions of photos. Max Howell (Creator of Homebrew) — whose self-directed open-source tool became the indispensable package manager for millions of macOS developers worldwide. David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) (Creator of Ruby on Rails & Co-founder of 37signals) — a Business Administration & Computer Science graduate who built one of the most influential web application frameworks entirely out of practical, real-world necessity. Seeing how these individuals bridged immense knowledge gaps through pure curiosity and self-driven execution convinced me that a formal degree was not the ultimate bottleneck.
Given my family’s financial situation at graduation, I decided against pursuing a traditional degree path and chose to commit entirely to self-learning. It was a lonely road from day one—my family couldn’t understand my choice, nor did they support me spending hours staring at a screen “messing around with code.”
Facing skepticism and cold shoulders, I bet everything on online learning resources.
2. From Web Dev to Autonomous Vehicles: My Self-Taught Tech Tree Without a prestigious computer science degree, Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) became my ultimate weapon.
I built my own step-by-step learning roadmap, soaking up knowledge across Coursera, edX, and Udacity:
🎯 My learning path at that time：
Front-End ➔ Full Stack ➔ Android Development ➔ Data Analyst ➔ Machine Learning ➔ Self-Driving Car
I tackled one domain after another—starting from simple front-end pages to building full-stack applications and Android apps, then mastering Python data analysis and machine learning.
Then I came across the Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree (SDCND) launched by Udacity founder Sebastian Thrun. Autonomous driving was at its absolute peak of technical excitement.
Back then, Udacity operated on a highly selective, application-based cohort model. With tech leaders racing to develop production-ready autonomous vehicles, over 11,000 applicants vied for just a few hundred spots—a daunting ~2–5% acceptance rate.
I applied immediately and was thrilled to be accepted into the second global cohort (November 2016). Surrounding me were brilliant peers hailing from elite tech giants like Google, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and AT&T, as well as top-tier institutions like MIT, Stanford, CMU, Princeton and NUS.
Learning alongside such extraordinary talent pushed me to my limits. After months of late-night coding and complex robotics projects, I officially graduated as part of the inaugural class of Udacity’s Self-Driving Car Engineers.
References & Further Viewing Udacity Official Landing Page & Original Syllabus: Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree (Archived 2016) | Download Official Program Syllabus (PDF)
Reuters Article: Udacity’s self-driving car engineering degree lures over 11,000 hopefuls
“The high number of applicants — for 250 spots in the course — underscores the pressing need for talent by technology leaders such as Alphabet’s Google and Apple, traditional car companies and automotive start-ups…”
Reddit (r/SelfDrivingCars): Did any of you who applied to the Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree program already get a mail that you are accepted?
“Everybody is in, split over different cohorts over the coming months: 500 for October, 1500 for November, 2500 for December… with 11,500 applicants in mind.”
Related Videos & Media NOVA PBS Documentary — The Great Robot Race (2005 DARPA Grand Challenge): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=saVZ_X9GfIM The historic NOVA documentary covering the legendary 2005 DARPA Grand Challenge, where Sebastian Thrun led the Stanford Racing Team to victory with “Stanley”—the robotic vehicle that catalyzed the modern autonomous vehicle revolution.
Oliver Cameron (CEO, Voyage & Former Udacity SDCND Lead) on MIT Self-Driving Cars: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j0tc0Y1CIE Oliver Cameron’s MIT guest lecture detailing how Udacity built and launched the SDCND program, how they deployed code to an actual Lincoln MKZ, and how those learnings laid the foundation for his autonomous taxi startup, Voyage.
Stanford AI Lab & Sebastian Thrun - DARPA Urban Challenge 2007 Documentary: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dHHppGy3p_c A fascinating deep-dive documentary following Sebastian Thrun and the Stanford Racing Team as they built “Junior” (a modified VW Passat) to navigate complex urban traffic, stop signs, and 360-degree sensor fusion in the 2007 DARPA challenge.
Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree Overview: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JkqmOUNbNfY The official program trailer led by Udacity curriculum lead David Silver and industry partners like Mercedes-Benz, breaking down the 3-term curriculum from Computer Vision and Sensor Fusion to Path Planning and ROS integration.
3. Why Udacity SDCND Was the Hardest Challenge for Me in 2017 If web development was about building user applications, SDCND in 2017 was hardcore low-level logic fused with cutting-edge algorithms. It demanded exceptional proficiency in C++ and Python, alongside heavy mathematical and physical modeling across three core pillars:
Computer Vision: Using OpenCV and deep learning to extract lane lines and detect traffic signs with extreme precision on image matrices. Sensor Fusion: Implementing Kalman Filters and Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) to fuse real-time noisy data from LiDAR and Radar. The mathematical derivations were unforgiving. Localization & Path Planning: Particle Filters, A* search algorithms, and control theory (PID control and Model Predictive Control). Every project required precise vehicle control inside simulated environments. Coming from a background with only a Diploma in Business Studies, the learning curve wasn’t a ramp—it was a vertical wall. I had to learn multivariate calculus, linear algebra, and physics on the fly while simultaneously optimizing performance in C++. To bridge the massive gap, I bought physical math textbooks and ground through supplemental courses on DataCamp and Khan Academy late into the night.
During this period, I also competed in MIT’s DeepTraffic competition (6.S094: Deep Learning for Self-Driving Cars), where I managed to secure the #1 spot on the global leaderboard. That achievement earned me a full Term 1 tuition-waiver scholarship for the Udacity SDCND, which provided a crucial boost to my learning journey.
At barely 20 years old, while my peers were enjoying traditional university life, I was the complete outlier. I had no safety net, very little money, and virtually no support system. Back in 2017, spending days locked in my room trying to “self-teach self-driving cars” sounded like a joke to the people around me. No one truly understood what I was building toward, and the isolation was heavy.
Yet, I gritted my teeth and kept going simply because I had no other choice. My days were defined by dozens of open Stack Overflow tabs, dense academic papers, and local C++ compiler errors. Every rejected project review tested my mental resilience to its absolute limit, but each resubmission pushed my engineering rigor to a level I never knew I was capable of achieving.
It was during this intense period of studying, building autonomous systems, and sharing my progress online that another incredible surprise occurred: NVIDIA AI officially followed my Instagram account.
4. Academic Rigor: Master’s-Level Recognition (NZQA) The sheer depth and academic rigor of this curriculum extended far beyond typical online certifications or light tutorial projects.
Rather than teaching basic scripting or superficial high-level frameworks, the program forced students to implement complex robotic algorithms entirely from scratch—ranging from non-linear sensor fusion with Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) to non-convex optimization in Model Predictive Control (MPC).
This level of depth did not go unnoticed by educational authorities. The New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) formally evaluated micro-credentials and benchmarked the Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree as equivalent to a 60-credit course at Level 9 (Master’s degree level) on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF).
🏛️ Official Government Recognition: As part of a national initiative to integrate emerging tech micro-credentials into formal education, New Zealand officially recognized top-tier industry programs like the SDCND as matching the academic depth and analytical rigor of post-graduate university studies.
Reference: New Zealand Government Release — New Zealand welcomes first micro-credentials
Understanding the Credential: Industry Value vs. Academic Scope To set realistic expectations, it is essential to distinguish between traditional academic credentialing and high-impact industry recognition. While the SDCND demands postgraduate-level intellect, its real-world execution operates under a modern tech paradigm:
Aspect Is it Recognized? What it Means in Practice Academic Accreditation ❌ No It is an industry-driven micro-credential rather than a accredited degree. It does not confer a formal university diploma, nor does it count toward university transferable credits. Tech & AV Industry Recognition ✅ Yes Recognized globally by premier autonomous vehicle teams and Silicon Valley giants (e.g., Waymo, Mercedes-Benz, NVIDIA, Cruise) who treat its project portfolio as equivalent to advanced graduate-level practical experience. Why Industry Weight Trumps Traditional Accreditation in AV For self-taught engineers and career switchers, this distinction proved to be an advantage rather than a drawback:
Emphasis on Hardcore Code, Not Paper Degrees: Autonomous driving engineering demands real, fault-tolerant C++ and Python code over theoretical exam scores. Autonomous vehicle engineering teams look directly at raw commit histories, simulation videos, and math derivations rather than university logos. Curriculum Agility: Traditional universities often take years to approve new course syllabi through academic committees. The SDCND, co-designed directly by active engineers at Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA, updated its codebase in real-time to reflect actual production stacks. The Proof is in the Portfolio: While the Nanodegree cannot replace a formal academic degree on paper, completing its master’s-level projects provided the concrete proof-of-work needed to bypass preliminary HR screenings and compete directly with CS master’s and Ph.D. graduates in technical interviews. 5. Why the First Cohort Carried So Much Weight The modern, revamped iterations of SDCND have lowered the barrier to entry significantly, but back then, the original curriculum took around a full year of grueling effort to get from admission to graduation. Being part of those inaugural batches meant stepping into a world with exceptionally high stakes and prestige:
Direct Collaboration with Tech Giants: This wasn’t just theoretical coursework. Led directly by Sebastian Thrun (“Father of the Self-Driving Car”), the program was co-developed with global pioneers and automotive leaders including Mercedes-Benz, NVIDIA, DiDi, Uber/Otto, and BMW. The curriculum was designed to mirror real-world production stacks, meaning graduation credentials carried immense weight across the autonomous driving ecosystem. A High-Filter Talent Pool: The original admissions process had a strict screening mechanism requiring detailed applications, code evaluations, and background reviews. Most of my peers in that initial group held Master’s or Ph.D. degrees from top-tier universities worldwide in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, or Robotics, or possessed years of professional hardware/software engineering experience. Many of my classmates were graduates from elite institutions like Stanford, MIT, and Carnegie Mellon—meanwhile, I entered with no formal CS background and a business diploma. Fast-Track Industry Pipelines: Thanks to deep partner involvement, early graduates received priority interviews and green-lit fast tracks at industry leaders like Waymo, Tesla, Cruise, Baidu Apollo, and DiDi. The vast majority of early alumni went on to become core R&D pillars at top AV startups and tech giants, solidifying the prestige of the initial SDCND badge. 5.1 Severe Talent Shortage: Hired Before Graduation Between 2016 and 2017, the global autonomous driving industry experienced an explosive technological frenzy. Traditional automakers and Silicon Valley giants were investing billions of dollars to build out AV teams, yet the entire industry faced a severe “zero supply” talent gap—at that time, virtually no universities offered dedicated degree programs specifically for autonomous vehicles.
Against this historic backdrop, students in the inaugural Udacity SDCND cohorts became some of the most sought-after talent in the entire tech ecosystem:
Hired Before Certificates Were Issued: Many outstanding students in our cohort were snapped up by major tech giants and AV unicorns before they even completed all three terms. Communities like our Slack channels and r/SelfDrivingCars were filled with weekly “Job Offer” success stories from students who landed roles after completing just Term 1 or Term 2. Project-Driven Recruitment: Passing the most demanding C++ and Python technical interviews often came down to showcasing high-quality project repositories (such as Behavioral Cloning or Extended Kalman Filters) on GitHub. A well-known example from our cohort was George Sung—originally a hardware/chip engineer who documented his career transition on his personal blog and in Udacity’s Medium feature, Becoming a Self-Driving Car Machine Learning Engineer. By leveraging his SDCND project code and active participation in the Slack community, he successfully landed a full-time role as an Autonomous Driving Engineer mid-way through the program, achieving a massive career leap. 5.2 Direct Access: Udacity’s Hiring Partner Network When designing the Nanodegree, founder Sebastian Thrun deliberately dismantled the barrier between traditional academia and industry. SDCND was never just an online course—it was built as an active recruitment pipeline for top-tier tech companies.
Udacity assembled an unprecedented Hiring Partner Network that included:
AV Pioneers & Tech Giants: NVIDIA, Uber ATG, DiDi, and Voyage. Traditional Automakers & Top Suppliers: Mercedes-Benz, BMW, and McLaren. These partners were deeply involved in both curriculum creation and talent acquisition:
Co-Developed Curriculum: Engineering teams from partner companies helped craft specific modules (for instance, the Mercedes-Benz team directly assisted in writing the tutorial for the Extended Kalman Filter sensor fusion module). Priority Resume Pipeline: Once students submitted passing project code, exceptional work was pushed into the Udacity Talent Source database. Partner recruiting teams could bypass initial HR screens to directly inspect students’ GitHub repos and simulation demonstration videos. Exclusive Recruitment Channels & Slack Access: Udacity hosted virtual career fairs exclusively for the first batch of students. Company CTOs and engineering leads regularly posted unlisted R&D roles directly inside dedicated Slack channels. For someone coming from a non-CS background with only a Diploma in Business Studies, this system was transformative. It evaluated candidates purely on hardcore coding skills, offering direct access to top global AV teams and allowing self-taught developers to compete on equal footing with engineering graduates from elite institutions worldwide.
6. Accelerating Ahead: Graduating with Batch 1 Although I was admitted as part of Batch 2, I poured nearly every waking hour into the coursework, pulling endless late-night sessions to complete the hardcore projects at breakneck speed.
My effort paid off: I caught up with the schedule and graduated alongside the very first global cohort (Batch 1)!
Because of this accomplishment, I received a personal invitation from Udacity founder and former Google Self-Driving Car pioneer Sebastian Thrun to attend the official graduation ceremony in the United States alongside graduates from around the world.
For a self-taught practitioner in their early 20s, it was an incredible validation and honor.
7. Regrets and Reflections: A Clear Conscience Reality, however, brought its own constraints.
In my early 20s with limited financial means, I simply couldn’t afford the flight and accommodation to the US. To make matters harder, my family still didn’t understand online education or autonomous driving, seeing it as an impractical pursuit.
Ultimately, I couldn’t attend that graduation ceremony across the ocean.
Do I have regrets? Absolutely. But do I regret the journey? Not for a second.
Going from a business student copying HTML snippets on W3Schools to a self-taught engineer implementing sensor fusion in C++ proved something invaluable:
It completely reshaped my learning methodology—proving that with the right drive, no technical ceiling is unbreachable. It gave me unshakeable technical confidence—if I could master self-driving algorithms, no new technology or framework could intimidate me again. Self-directed learning can be a lonely road marked by doubt and real-world hurdles. But once you write that first line of code and keep going, every late night and effort spent becomes the strongest armor you carry forward.
summary:
If I had to choose the most brutally difficult course in my entire self-learning journey, it would undoubtedly be the Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree (SDCND).

Born in 1996 with only a Diploma in Business Studies, I had zero Computer Science (CS) background. I had never taken university-level advanced math or higher physics. Yet, I not only conquered this Autonomous Driving program—a course that leaves many CS master’s students struggling—but also became one of its top early graduates globally.
title: The Hardest Online Course I Ever Took

Programming a Real Self-Driving Car (Team Project) Our team implemented key functionalities like perception (object detection, traffic light recognition), planning (path planning, behavioral decision making), and control (steering, throttle control) using ROS, Python, and C++.
Team Members: Anton Pechenko, Kai Detlefsen, Andrew Ayers, Muddassir Ahmed Khan, Ng Fang Kiang (Me)
At age 21, I had the privilege of collaborating with top-tier engineers who later progressed into key industry roles, including Head of AI at Giant.AI, Quant Researcher at IMC Trading, AI Engineer at Vesoma (physical AI startups), and Senior Engineers at Callsign & Unified Compliance.
Identify and Track a Target in Simulation with Deep Learning This project uses deep learning to train a model that can identify and track a target (like a vehicle) within a simulated environment. The model learns from simulated data and then utilizes computer vision techniques to detect and follow the target in real-time, showcasing object recognition and tracking capabilities.
Advanced Lane Lines Detection The Advanced Lane Lines Detection project uses computer vision techniques like camera calibration, distortion correction, color/gradient thresholding, perspective transform, and sliding window search to reliably identify lane lines in a video stream, even under challenging conditions like shadows or varying road curvature.
Rover - Search and Sample Return I developed a simulated autonomous rover using Python to navigate a simulated Martian environment. The rover employed image processing techniques, including color thresholding and perspective transforms, along with path planning algorithms to identify rock samples and return them to the base. This project resulted in successful navigation and sample retrieval.
Robotic Arm - Pick & Place Project In this project, I calculated the forward and inverse kinematics of a 6-DOF robotic arm to enable autonomous pick-and-place functionality in a ROS/Gazebo simulation environment. Using Python and NumPy, the robotic arm successfully identified target objects, calculated motion trajectories, and performed accurate pick and place operations.
Jorcus - Global Remote Work Platform Jorcus is a cross-platform community and marketplace designed to connect remote workers worldwide. It offers dedicated job boards, remote working guides, and a unified ecosystem across Web, Mobile, and Desktop.

content:
Back in December 2021, I wrote a post outlining what I believed the world and the tech landscape would look like over the next five years. Looking around today in 2026, it’s fascinating—and deeply satisfying—to see how many of those predictions have shifted from bold foresight into everyday reality.
Here is a look back at what I wrote in 2021, alongside how those trends have actually played out:
1. The Work Revolution: Remote, Automation, and “Workations” What I predicted in 2021: Remote and hybrid work would become standard, manual labor would transition into configuring AI/robots, and terms like “Workation” and “digital nomad” would mainstream as live, work, and travel integrate. The Reality in 2026: Work is no longer tied to a physical office for millions. The line between living and working has blurred into a modern digital nomad lifestyle. On the industrial side, automation and applied AI have taken over repetitive physical labor, transforming modern manual roles into high-tech operator and supervisory positions. 2. AI & Software Development: Software 2.0 & AI Assistance What I predicted in 2021: Software development would pivot heavily toward concepts like Software 2.0, GitHub Copilot, and early LLMs (like GPT-3). The Reality in 2026: AI-assisted development is no longer an experiment; it is the fundamental way code is written today. Developers have evolved into architects driving AI systems, dramatically accelerating how products are built and deployed. 3. Hardware & Infrastructure: ARM Chips, 5G, and PWA Adoption What I predicted in 2021: ARM architecture and 5G would dominate computation, while Web-based PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) would gain ground as native app fatigue set in. The Reality in 2026: ARM has solidified its place as the efficiency benchmark across both mobile devices and cloud servers. Connectivity is seamless, and lightweight, web-centric software models continue to challenge bloated native applications. 4. Digital Humans, Virtual Reality, & Spatial Computing What I predicted in 2021: Virtual/digital humans (like @lilmiquela) would become mainstream influencers alongside traditional YouTubers and KOLs, while AR/VR technologies would gain widespread adoption. The Reality in 2026: Virtual avatars and AI-driven personalities are everywhere in digital marketing, gaming, and content creation. Spatial computing and immersive 3D experiences are integrated deeply into everyday entertainment and media. 5. Sustainability & Electric Vehicles What I predicted in 2021: Electric vehicles (EVs) would be enforced and prioritized to save the planet. The Reality in 2026: The global shift away from traditional ICE engines has accelerated rapidly, making EVs the default choice for new drivers around the world. Final Thoughts As I noted back in 2021: “The future is not something to be feared, but something to be embraced.” Seeing these shifts materialize over the last five years reinforces that technology moves fast, but clear trajectory markers are almost always visible if we look closely enough.
Now, as we look toward the next horizon, emerging fields like biocomputing, advanced biomachines, and deeper AI integrations are calling. The next decade promises to be even more transformative.
Original Author: Ng Fang Kiang
Original Post (Published December 5, 2021):
The future is not something to be feared, but something to be embraced. There’s an inherent danger in clinging to progress, but progress is precisely the reason we should be embracing it.
In the next 5 years, I think a lot of things will change.
I think remote work is here to stay. People continue to work remotely (fully remote or hybrid work). For manual workers, It’s very likely to transform into another job that requires some engineer skills to configure the AI/robots that works with the industry. Hybrid work is for some industry or people that need time for transition to fully remote. For those job required to work in a certain place are still exists, but will start to replace by automation robots (AGV, AIoT, Applied AI, self-driving car and so on)
Zero-trust security is crucial. Like E2E encryption, blockchain, NFT and so on.
With the embrace of VR and AR technologies. The terms of “virtual human” or “digital human” like @lilmiquela will become the norm just like the KOL, internet influencer or YouTuber in the next 5 years.
The future of programming? Maybe Software 2.0, Copilot, GPT-3, etc?
For internet and computation industry, I believe 5G and ARM chips will be the future.
For Android and iOS, I think a web base PWA app is more realistic in the next 5 years. People are now less likely to install lots of app into their phone even their phones are getting more powerful every single year.
For things like Windows 11, the WinUI3 seems very promising. I think Windows 11 might be another big thing in the next 5 years.
I think people will have more time to travel and work. Things like “Workation”, “Staycation”, “digital nomad” will get popularize. Live, work, and travel used to be separate, but now they are all integrated.
Look ahead for the 5 to 10 years. I believe something like metaverse, omniverse, AR, VR, all kind of 3D stuffs (Simulation,3D/4D printing,3Dmovie/news, Technologies) and so on will be popularized and became another norm. Electric vehicles will be enforced. Save the planet without more gasoline! Flying car seems very promising too! Until that time, I think I will start to look at something like biomachine, biocomputing and so on.

content:
Back in early 2017, I had the incredible opportunity to participate in MIT’s 6.S094: Deep Learning for Self-Driving Cars competition—DeepTraffic. Hosted via the official MIT DeepTraffic Simulator, it was an exhilarating experience that marked a significant milestone in my journey with AI and autonomous driving technology.
This competition proved to be the ultimate catalyst for my tech career: it earned me a tuition waiver for the Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree, put my social handle on the map, and eventually led to NVIDIA AI following my Instagram account.
Leaderboard Achievements DeepTraffic 1.0 Leaderboard DeepTraffic 1.1 Leaderboard View Full-Res Screenshot ↗ View Full-Res Screenshot ↗ Achieving #1 on DeepTraffic 1.0 & 1.1 In January 2017, after countless hours of hyperparameter tuning, model iteration, and deep reinforcement learning experiments, I managed to reach the #1 spot on the DeepTraffic 1.0 leaderboard under the username Instagram: Jorcus96 with a speed score of 75.38 MPH.
My #1 rank under instagram:jorcus96 was even captured in third-party write-ups and repositories at the time, such as Jason Salas’s Medium article on beating DeepTraffic and pranz24’s MIT-DeepTraffic-1.1 GitHub repository screenshot.
Just a month later, in February 2017, MIT released DeepTraffic 1.1, opening the competition to participants worldwide beyond MIT-registered students. The competition was even fiercer, but my optimized RL strategies paid off once again—I reclaimed the #1 spot on the DeepTraffic 1.1 leaderboard with an improved score of 75.82 MPH!
While waiting to hear back about the rewards, I pushed my model even further and achieved another top rank after hitting an even higher score of 76.16 MPH in February. After reaching that milestone, I decided to wrap up my work on the competition. Eventually, other participants surpassed that score, but my result remained in the Top 3 for nearly a year until the online competition was officially taken down from the website. Fortunately, the leaderboard was preserved on the Web Archive (captured on October 18, 2017), where my name is still visible.
Web Archive snapshot of the DeepTraffic 1.1 Leaderboard (saved October 18, 2017) showing NG FANG KIANG at Rank 3 with a score of 76.16 MPH. MIT DeepTraffic Lecture & Competition Overview To understand the core concepts behind DeepTraffic and how deep reinforcement learning is applied to motion planning, you can watch the official MIT 6.S094 lecture video below:
For further details on the underlying simulation engine, deep Q-learning environment, and parameters, check out the official MIT DeepTraffic GitHub repository.
Years later, Lex Fridman and his co-authors formally published the research paper “DeepTraffic: Crowdsourced Hyperparameter Tuning of Deep Reinforcement Learning Systems for Multi-Agent Dense Traffic Navigation” (arXiv:1801.02805), detailing how thousands of participants crowdsourced the search space for RL agent parameters in dense traffic simulations.
Turning Achievements into Opportunities After securing the top rank on both leaderboards, I took screenshots of my rankings and shared them with potential sponsors to showcase my passion and technical competence in self-driving technology.
That effort yielded an unbelievable result: I was awarded a one-term tuition waiver for the Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree—generously provided by the CEO of a prominent autonomous driving startup and former VP of Udacity!
This scholarship opened the doors to the hardest online course I ever took. Little did I know that branding my username as Instagram: Jorcus96 on the MIT leaderboard would also spark a chain reaction on social media, leading to NVIDIA AI following me on Instagram shortly after!
Key Takeaways Looking back, this experience taught me two important lessons:
Persistence in AI/RL Experiments: Fine-tuning reinforcement learning models requires patience, systematic trial-and-error, and deep understanding of agent-environment interactions. Showcasing Your Work Matters: Achieving something is great, but actively sharing your achievements, branding your work, and reaching out to supporters/sponsors can unlock opportunities you might never have imagined. Thank you to MIT for hosting such an awesome benchmark competition and to everyone who supported me throughout this journey!

Official Competition Code: MIT DeepTraffic Open Source Repository on GitHub DeepTraffic 1.0 Verification: Leaderboard Proof Screenshot (GitHub Repository) DeepTraffic 1.1 Verification: Leaderboard Proof Screenshot (GitHub Repository) Web Archive Leaderboard: MIT 6.S094 DeepTraffic 1.1 Archived Leaderboard (Oct 18, 2017) (showing NG FANG KIANG at Rank 3 with 76.16 MPH nearly a year later) Third-Party Community Write-up: My Attempt at Beating DeepTraffic by Jason Salas (featuring instagram:jorcus96 at #1 on the leaderboard screenshot) Third-Party GitHub Repository: pranz24’s MIT-DeepTraffic-1.1 Repository (capturing jorcus96 at #1 on the leaderboard)

Back in July 2017, when NVIDIA AI (@nvidiaai) launched its official Instagram account, something completely unexpected happened: they followed my personal account.
At the time, @nvidiaai was right at its inception with only a few dozen followers. I was going by my handle @jorcus96. Seeing an official account from a silicon and AI powerhouse pop up in my notifications felt completely surreal.
Connecting the Dots: How Did NVIDIA AI Find Me? Looking back at 2017, this unexpected connection was actually the culmination of a wild few months in the autonomous driving and AI space:
The MIT DeepTraffic Benchmark: In early 2017, I achieved the #1 spot globally in MIT’s 6.S094 DeepTraffic competition under the handle Instagram: Jorcus96. The leaderboard was widely shared across tech blogs, research repos, and social media. Udacity SDCND & NVIDIA Partnership: Winning DeepTraffic landed me a full scholarship for the Udacity Self-Driving Car Engineer Nanodegree. NVIDIA was one of Udacity’s primary co-developers for the program, actively monitoring top-performing students and community contributors on Slack, GitHub, and social channels. Active Tech Sharing: I was actively sharing my deep learning experiments, C++ sensor fusion code, and AI projects under @jorcus96. When NVIDIA AI set up their official account to track emerging talent, influential publications, and AI pioneers, my handle happened to be right in the middle of that ecosystem.
A Front-Row Seat to Early AI History By June 2019, as captured in the screenshots above, the account had grown to 4,278 followers across 65 posts, while keeping its following list exceptionally exclusive at just 135 accounts.
Scrolling through that select list, my personal handle (@jorcus96 / Ng Fang Kiang) sat right alongside prominent tech media outlets and institutes like Futurism Health, Explorist, Futurism Energy, Futurism Science, Curiosity Rover, TechCrunch, and MIT Technology Review.
As @nvidiaai scaled into a major industry hub with hundreds of thousands of followers, they eventually overhauled their social media strategy and unfollowed individual accounts. But having a front-row seat to the early days of official AI social media—and knowing that my self-taught journey in AI caught the eye of NVIDIA—remains one of my favorite pieces of personal tech trivia.
